answer.label: Paraphrase of Thoreau — not his exact words
answer.sourceLine: The thought is genuinely Thoreau’s, but the exact popular wording is not. Biographer Robert D. Richardson Jr. coined it in Henry Thoreau: A Life of the Mind (1986), p. 171, as a paraphrase of what Thoreau actually wrote in his Journal of 5 August 1851: “The question is not what you look at, but what you see.”

source.excerpt: The question is not what you look at, but what you see.
trail: The Walden Woods Project’s Thoreau Mis-Quotation Page ↗ lists this exact wording as a misquotation and gives Thoreau’s real Journal line of 5 August 1851.
Biographer Robert D. Richardson Jr. ↗ (1934–2020) wrote the streamlined version in Henry Thoreau: A Life of the Mind (1986), p. 171 — clearly paraphrasing Thoreau, not quoting him.
It nonetheless circulates verbatim under Thoreau’s name across the web, e.g. on Goodreads ↗, while his real line appears separately ↗.
source.cutTag: ↑ Thoreau posed it as a question; the popular version smooths it into a maxim
source.excerptNote: Thoreau framed the idea as a question about perception in his private Journal. The familiar declarative line — “It’s not what you look at that matters, it’s what you see” — is the later paraphrase that now circulates under his name.

author.name: Henry David Thoreau
author.heading: Henry David Thoreau
author.bio: Henry David Thoreau (1817–1862) was an American essayist, poet and naturalist, best known for Walden (1854) and the essay Civil Disobedience. His private Journal, kept for nearly a quarter-century and running to some two million words, is the true home of many lines later polished by others into popular quotations. The observation about looking versus seeing is authentically his — but the crisp maxim that circulates today is a modern biographer’s rewording of it.

misattribution.heading: The attribution problem
misattribution.intro: The line is universally credited to Thoreau as a verbatim quotation. It isn’t one — it’s a paraphrase, and Thoreau’s actual words are subtly different.

items.scope: Credited as a verbatim quote to
items.why: Thoreau never wrote these exact words. His Journal of 5 August 1851 reads “The question is not what you look at, but what you see” — a question, not the declarative “It’s not what you look at that matters” maxim now attached to him, as the Walden Woods Project ↗ documents.

misattribution.truthLine: Bottom line: the idea is Thoreau’s, but the exact wording is biographer Robert D. Richardson Jr.’s 1986 paraphrase ↗, not a Thoreau quotation.

context.heading: Why it drifted
lead: Thoreau’s Journal is a quotation minefield: it is vast, aphoristic, and mostly out of copyright, so writers routinely lift and tighten its sentences. The looking-versus-seeing line is a textbook case — Thoreau’s hedged, questioning original became a punchy motivational maxim once a biographer reformulated it.

Because Richardson’s Henry Thoreau: A Life of the Mind is one of the most widely read Thoreau biographies, his paraphrase spread as if it were Thoreau’s own words, and it now dominates search results, posters, and photography captions.
context.pull: Thoreau asked a question; the internet turned it into a slogan.
